The research utilizes two distinct sepsis datasets, each containing over 20,000 patient records, to simulate a federated learning environment. The primary objective is to determine if a DNN trained across a network of hospitals via a simple and efficient FL framework can outperform models trained on individual hospital data in isolation. Key challenges addressed include managing non-IID data distributions, addressing data sparsity, and handling class imbalance. Performance metrics across the hospital network demonstrate an average improvement of 10% in both discrimination and generalization. Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome resulting from a dysregulated systemic inflammatory reaction to infection, which leads to organ dysfunction and significant mortality. The condition is notoriously difficult to diagnose due to a lack of specific biomarkers and a complex, evolving disease trajectory. This paper investigates whether deep neural networks (DNNs) can leverage electronic health records (EHRs) to accurately identify sepsis patients. The study is based on a retrospective analysis of more than 1.1 million patient visits across 12 U.S. hospitals. The dataset was partitioned into a training set comprising 9 hospitals and a testing set consisting of 3 hospitals with no overlapping patients. The results show that a DNN trained on a single hospital achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.80 in identifying sepsis cases. By incorporating a domain adaptation technique, the model's generalization capability to the testing hospitals was significantly improved, reaching an AUC of 0.87. Additionally, the study identified 1,000 high-dimensional features that effectively distinguish sepsis patients from others.

In this Letter, we demonstrate that the flow of a viscous fluid can be fully reconstructed from the spatial anisotropies of its initial state, provided the fluid possesses a sufficiently large sound velocity. This finding is established using a holographic QCD model that encompasses both strong coupling and finite viscosity. The relevant ratio of a viscous fluid's sound velocity to the speed of light in a vacuum is determined by a parameter within the underlying holographic theory; this same parameter governs the degree of elliptic flow. We conclude by outlining the implications of these results for interpreting flow measurements in heavy-ion collisions.

a novel representation for rendering and editing both unordered point clouds and ordered meshes. An NDF defines a hidden semantic space relative to the current geometry, enabling the synthesis of new views and the deformation of geometry to resemble a target shape. The descriptor field is formulated as the gradient descent step required to transform one geometry into another within this latent space. Consequently, rendering and editing function as gradient descent tasks that minimize a perceptual loss on an image discriminator, offering a unified and efficient framework for generating novel viewpoints, downsampling point clouds, and performing editing operations such as relighting, resizing, rotating, and shape modification. Our results demonstrate that NDFs produce rendering quality comparable to recent view-dependent representations while substantially reducing memory usage. Furthermore, experiments on synthetic and real objects indicate that our method effectively generalizes across various pose and shape variations. Finally, we show that representing multiple poses and shapes using a single descriptor is more effective for editing than our prior field-based approach, as it facilitates the preservation of high-frequency details. The code is accessible at https://shyop-lab.github.io/ndf/.

Leveraging the unique capabilities of the JWST, we have extracted over 100 elemental abundances for 50 stars by employing both automated and manual techniques. Our findings indicate that the cluster exhibits a predominantly metal-rich population with a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] = -0.09 $\pm$ 0.07, characterized by a small dispersion in stellar abundances. We observe a significant alpha-element enhancement, with [alpha/Fe] = +0.25 $\pm$ 0.05, suggesting an enhanced rate of Type II supernovae. Furthermore, our data reveals a mild depletion in iron-peak elements and nitrogen enrichment, indicative of extensive first dredge-up effects. The heavy element distribution shows a bimodal pattern, with one mode attributed to the bulge's r-process pollution. Our results demonstrate that the 47 Tucanae cluster is highly chemically homogeneous, with minimal scatter in the abundances of most elements. However, we identify a distinct group of Na-O anti-cycle stars, which we attribute to binary mass transfer events. Finally, we note that the majority of the observed scatter in elemental abundances is attributable to the second dredge-up process. These insights provide a deeper understanding of the chemical evolution of the 47 Tucanae cluster and the Galactic bulge. Additionally, the high-quality data and methods established in this study will serve as a benchmark for analyzing the chemical composition of the Galactic bulge using the upcoming JWST/NIRSpec Time Series program.

In this work, we derive a bulk effective action for color superfluids using the four-loop four-fermion four-helicity projection within the functional renormalization group (FRG) framework. This derivation incorporates the effects of quark loops, quark masses, and finite chemical potential. We determine the flow of the four-fermion coupling and identify the superfluid phases characterized by the lowest energy, along with the boundary conditions for phase transitions. The proposed technique employs a single approximation network to replace computationally demanding posterior calculations within standard Bayesian inference. In recent years, significant advancements have been made in single-cell sequencing technologies, enabling researchers to measure gene expression across individual cells. These capabilities have facilitated high-dimensional analyses of cell-to-cell variability and the identification of distinct cell types and states. However, these measurements are inherently noisy, and the high dimensionality of gene expression data often complicates statistical modeling and statistical learning tasks. This work examines gene expression datasets from two different conditions and applies a modeling framework designed to improve learning about a specific condition by leveraging information from the other. We demonstrate that this approach yields more accurate estimates of a cell's transcriptome under a single condition and produces more precise clustering results compared to baselines. Furthermore, the method effectively scales to experiments involving thousands of cells. We open-source the code at https://github.com/brandonpugh/TEB.

We introduce a new approach for clustering single-cell gene expression data, addressing the challenge of high dimensionality and noise inherent in these measurements. The method utilizes a two-component mixture model to account for gene expression distributions, incorporating a correlation network to capture dependencies among genes. By integrating a random walk process along this correlation network, the technique infers cell types under a semi-supervised learning paradigm. This strategy allows the algorithm to benefit from reference cell type information found in other datasets. We validate the method's performance through simulations and real-world data, showing that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/brandonpugh/TEB.

These structures are increasingly recognized for their potential to solve complex challenges across diverse fields, including white-light nanoimaging, super-resolution imaging, supercoupling, cloaking, and superlensing. This paper introduces a metasurface design featuring square metallic patches on both sides of a dielectric substrate, utilizing magnesium fluoride (MgF₂) as the substrate material. The metasurface functions as a phase converter, transforming planar electromagnetic waves into conical waves. We present a general analytical method to calculate the cone angle, demonstrating that this angle is independent of the incident angle and frequency. Furthermore, the surface impedance is derived analytically to determine the optimal geometric parameters. Numerical simulations confirm that a single metasurface can transform a plane wave into a conical wave, while two such surfaces enable the conversion between plane and cone waves. Additionally, we illustrate how a single metasurface can transform a divergent beam into a convergent beam. gamma-ray burst, GCs~20200210, originating from a Galactic globular cluster (GCs~NGC~6397) using the 2.6-meter fiber-fed spectrograph of the Liverpool Telescope. This event, which exhibited an optical peak magnitude of $V\sim19.5$, was analyzed through both optical and near-infrared data, revealing a spectrum characterized by high metallicity and an intermediate effective temperature. The observed properties, particularly the spectrum's shape and the derived metallicity, align with the expectation that the transient destroyed a red giant star within its host cluster. This marks the first identification of a Galactic transient with an intermediate-mass progenitor. Based on the event's optical characteristics, we propose that GCs~20200210 represents a novel class of transients, potentially termed "cluster gamma-ray bursts." This discovery offers a unique opportunity to investigate the intra-cluster environment, the specific conditions required for such cluster gamma-ray bursts, and their implications for the evolution of stellar populations in Galactic globular clusters. Furthermore, the ability to identify these events via optical spectroscopy suggests that future wide-field surveys, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time, could detect similar transients. Finally, we note that the light curve of GCs~20200210 resembles that of AT~2019dli, a tidal disruption event (TDE) with an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) progenitor; however, the significantly higher luminosity of the gamma-ray emission in this event suggests that an IMBH is not the source of the gamma-rays. This study investigates the sensitivity and detectability of photometric variability in stellar populations that host planets with diverse atmospheric compositions and circulation patterns. We simulate synthetic JWST observations of these populations, incorporating both radiative and dynamical effects, to assess potential biosignatures and atmospheric indicators. Our results demonstrate that JWST can identify photometric fluctuations caused by radiative features, such as the condensate sign, in synthetic surveys of nearby G and K-type stars. This paper introduces a novel PD framework specifically designed for polymers undergoing large deformations. The proposed model accounts for both elastic and inelastic behaviors, with inelastic effects encompassing rate-dependent viscoelasticity, thermal expansion, and damage. To solve the resulting highly nonlinear peridynamic equations of motion, an implicit time integration scheme is employed, utilizing a mixed finite element method to discretize displacements and internal thermal stresses separately. This mixed approach effectively manages volumetric locking during finite strain simulations. To accelerate the solution process, a modified Newton-Raphson iteration is implemented, incorporating an enhanced tangent operator and a line search strategy. To validate the model, validation tests are conducted on a polymer sheet, and subsequent applications explore the failure mechanisms of polymer films under tensile loading and the impact response of three-dimensional polymer structures. These applications demonstrate that the model can accurately capture diverse phenomena, including damage initiation and propagation, plastic dissipation, thermal softening, large deformations, and material fragmentation. The results obtained from this model show strong agreement with experimental data and conventional continuum mechanics predictions.

Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) extend standard linear regression to handle non-normal distributions and transformed variables. They establish a connection between the expected value of the response variable and linear predictors through a link function, utilizing a probability density function from the exponential family. This approach offers a straightforward yet powerful framework for statistical analysis across diverse fields.

However, their use introduces a significant drawback: the plastic generates nonlinear acoustic noise that interferes with imaging. While prior studies have explored replacing PMMA with aluminum or acrylic glass (Plexiglas), these alternatives fail to replicate the focal length achievable with standard PMMA lenses. Ultrasound radiation force enables the manipulation of microscale objects, a capability that has been harnessed to trap and move microbeads, red blood cells, and microbubbles. A key factor in optimizing this technique is the focal length of the ultrasound source. Although PMMA acoustic lenses are commonly used to focus ultrasound, they introduce acoustic noise due to nonlinear distortion. Current solutions, such as using materials like aluminum or Plexiglas, result in focal lengths that are significantly longer than those provided by PMMA. This paper introduces a novel approach to achieve an adjustable focal length while maintaining the compact size offered by PMMA lenses. The method involves temporarily lowering the glass transition temperature ($T_g$) of the PMMA lens to make it flexible, allowing the focal length to be tuned within the range of 1.5 cm to 10 cm. This technique offers a cost-effective and compact solution for generating focused ultrasound beams with variable focal lengths.

of quantum complexity, referred to as "mid-circuit measurement" quantum complexity. This approach builds upon the Fidelity Sandwich Recipe (FSR), which utilizes a two-parameter "sandwich" protocol to evaluate states evolving under unitary dynamics. The "mid-circuit measurement" FSR differs slightly from the original FSR, applying the same core concept to measure the complexity of quantum operations themselves rather than quantum states. We demonstrate that this protocol yields a monotonically increasing metric for unitary complexity and numerically estimate the value of complexity for random unitary circuits matching previous findings. Furthermore, we show how to incorporate constraints into the computation of mid-circuit measurement quantum complexity. A significant advantage of this protocol is its applicability to both closed and open quantum systems, enabling the study of quantum error correction and error mitigation, as well as determining the efficiency of fault-tolerant logical gates. We anticipate that the mid-circuit measurement FSR will serve as a vital tool for investigating quantum complexity in future experimental settings.

The process is divided into three distinct phases: initial impact, surface seal, and oscillation. Initial impact involves shock generation and the formation of a high-pressure, high-velocity jet at the pole of the sphere. In the surface seal phase, the rear of the sphere acts as an orifice, producing a downward jet that interacts with the free surface to create an expanding air cavity. The seal phase duration depends on the ratio between the rear jet velocity and the surface elevation. During the oscillation phase, the rear jet periodically pierces the free surface, while the front jet repeatedly impacts it. The interplay of these jets and the rear orifice diameter dictates the surface dynamics. When the rear jet penetrates the surface, the front jet elevates it; conversely, when the front jet impacts the surface, the rear jet fails to pierce it. This interaction induces an oscillating surface seal, where the air cavity rhythmically expands and collapses. The collapse generates a high-pressure shock, causing the cavity to rebound and expand again. These findings are validated through direct numerical simulations (DNS) of incompressible water and compressible air, which accurately reproduce the simulated pressures and shock structures observed in water-air interface experiments. The simulations also reveal that the rebound time is directly proportional to the cavity volume at the moment of collapse. Additionally, the study shows that the rear jet velocity is independent of the sphere's angular velocity $\omega$, whereas the surface elevation is influenced by $\omega$. This influence is more pronounced at lower Froude numbers and becomes negligible at higher Froude numbers. Furthermore, the impact pressure at the pole is independent of $\omega$. However, at moderate $\omega$, the pressure at the rear of the sphere is sensitive to $\omega$, whereas at high $\omega$, it becomes independent. This pressure distribution influences the rear jet velocity and the onset of surface oscillations. Finally, DNS results indicate that the non-dimensional pressure coefficient at the rear of the sphere is governed by the Reynolds number. These conclusions are supported by both experimental and numerical evidence. The research offers insights into optimizing the conditions for creating underwater cavities, which is critical for applications such as underwater shock wave generation, hydrofoil water entry

While this has been rigorously proven for Abelian charges in non-chiral theories and for all charges in quantum field theories with linearly realized symmetries, the scenario for non-Abelian, chiral global symmetries remains unexamined. This work demonstrates that the consistent anomaly associated with an effective operator linking two Higgs doublets gives rise to an anomalous global $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_B$ symmetry. While static analysis and machine learning have been employed to detect these exploits, they struggle with the vast array of potential leak behaviors and frequently yield inaccurate results. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a static analysis approach that leverages the visual, audio, and network contexts to identify data leaks. Our method involves reverse engineering the target application to construct a precise intermediate representation, followed by analyzing how the application's state changes in response to various inputs. This approach successfully pinpoints data leaks that previous methods failed to detect. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our technique operates with high efficiency, capable of identifying leaks in most applications without the need for user-provided examples. In extensive evaluations on 1,000 open-source apps, our method discovered 1,000 previously unknown leaks, a finding that was further validated on an additional 1,000 apps containing known vulnerabilities. These results demonstrate that reverse engineering is a viable and effective strategy for uncovering a significant volume of previously undetected data leaks.

Applications that rely on third-party plugins or extensions often suffer from security flaws that are difficult to uncover using conventional analysis techniques. These issues are challenging to detect because the behavior of the main application is heavily influenced by the plugins, and the problematic interactions typically manifest only during runtime. Consequently, reverse engineering and testing are essential for discovery, yet they are extremely difficult due to the sheer volume and diversity of possible plugin combinations. We present a solution that integrates automated dynamic analysis with a lightweight, learning-based approach. This system automatically discovers and characterizes leak behaviors through a "curriculum learning" process, starting with simple behaviors and progressively moving to complex ones. By doing so, it overcomes the constraints of traditional dynamic analysis, which are hindered by the infinite variety of potential execution paths and the lack of a comprehensive intermediate representation for all behaviors. This automated system uncovered 1,000 previously unknown leaks in a survey of 1,000 apps containing at least one verified leak. These leaks were subsequently categorized into 14 distinct types, with 11 types being novel. The identified leaks span multiple contexts, including visual, audio, network, and battery usage.

We address a novel extension of standard linear stochastic bandits, termed "shifted linear bandits," where the learner observes a sequence of features and selects actions to maximize expected reward. However, due to an adversarial shift, the observed rewards deviate from their true distribution. The objective is to learn as quickly as possible to identify a positive linear combination of the mean observed rewards. The learner faces a bounded total budget of noisy observations and remains ignorant of the true mean reward distribution for every possible action. We demonstrate a $\sqrt{T}$-suboptimal regret lower bound for any algorithm and provide an explicit strategy that achieves this result.

This paper introduces a new framework for robust reinforcement learning called the Team Game, designed to handle a bounded number of noisy transitions and rewards. The learner is granted an oblivious but constrained adversary with a finite total budget of noisy steps. Motivated by learning control in linear systems, the learner's goal is to minimize cumulative loss over $T$ steps. The team game connects closely with prior work on bounded budgets and offers improved sample complexity for solving linear systems. We prove that the learner can achieve a $\sqrt{T}$-suboptimal excess regret against the adversary, alongside an optimal $d^2/T$ mean squared error. Furthermore, we show that $\sqrt{T}$-suboptimal excess regret is attainable even with a constant number of noisy steps.

The discovery of choice-based superforecasts was unexpected, as was the fact that forecaster choices are not the primary driver of their success. BaTiO$_3$ is a perovskite ferroelectric material renowned for its exceptional dielectric properties, which have spurred extensive research into its structural phases and electronic band structure. Although the crystal structure can adopt various phases depending on temperature and pressure, the most prevalent are the paraelectric cubic (Pm$\bar{3}$m) and the primary ferroelectric phases: tetragonal (P4mm), orthorhombic (mm2), and rhombohedral (m3m). As temperature decreases from the high-temperature cubic phase, BaTiO$_3$ sequentially transitions into the orthorhombic, rhombohedral, and tetragonal phases before eventually reaching the paraelectric cubic state at elevated temperatures. Figure~\ref{fig:phase_diagram} illustrates the phase diagram of BaTiO$_3$ as a function of temperature and pressure, incorporating both experimental and theoretical data. Notably, the pressure-induced transition points between these phases are significantly lower than those observed at ambient pressure.

In this study, we employ {\it ab initio} band structure calculations to investigate the pressure-dependent phase transitions of BaTiO$_3$. Our results indicate that the transition pressures derived from these calculations are in good agreement with existing experimental data. Moreover, we examine the band structures of both the ambient pressure phase and the high-pressure phase, revealing that the pressure-induced changes in the electronic structure align well with previous findings. This confirms that the underlying mechanism of the pressure-induced phase transition in BaTiO$_3$ is band-gap engineering.

While various theoretical frameworks have been developed to address specific material systems, a unified model capable of explaining multi-phonon effects across different contexts remains absent. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Boson-Holstein-Scalapino (BHS) model, which integrates key phenomena such as multi-phonon scattering, excitation generation, and annihilation. Accompanying this model is a solvable two-level system that offers qualitative insights into its physics. We present a general approach to calculate scattering rates and generate scattering graphs for both two- and three-body processes. Applied to an Ar$_4$@He experiment, this application successfully reproduces the observed peak position and shape within a two-body BHS band. These findings demonstrate that the BHS model effectively captures multi-body multi-phonon effects, providing a robust framework for interpreting future pre- and post-peaks data. Finally, we propose that the BHS model could similarly address multi-magnon and multi-magphonon effects. The source code for the two- and three-body BHS model applications is available at https://github.com/andrewjgarcia/BHS.

We demonstrate that the BHS model can accurately predict previously unobserved peaks in helium-solvated argon clusters.

Because these problems typically involve a large number of constraints relative to their variables, standard solvers often struggle with convergence, computational efficiency, and memory usage. This paper introduces a novel class of penalty methods designed to address this specific category of problems. These penalties are constructed by exploiting the integral structure inherent in the constraints, enabling formulation as a system of algebraic equations and inequalities. This approach allows the problem to be solved with significantly higher computational speed and reduced memory requirements compared to traditional approaches. Test cases drawn from engineering applications, such as parameter estimation and optimal control, demonstrate the method's advantages. Furthermore, the relationship between the solution sets of the original constrained problem, the standard penalty method, and this new approach is examined. The study concludes with suggestions for future enhancements, including solving the resulting system using interior point methods and extending the framework to include equality constraints.

In recent years, significant advancements have been made in solving optimization problems using model predictive control techniques. A primary obstacle in applying these methods to systems governed by differential equations is the high computational cost associated with integrating these equations during each iteration of numerical solvers. This document presents a new strategy for reducing computational time when addressing real-time optimal control and estimation problems using model predictive control. The approach involves developing a novel algorithm capable of efficiently solving the necessary conditions for optimality expressed as differential algebraic equations. This algorithm is also applicable to sparse optimization problems. To validate the method, the document compares a specific implementation against modeltroubader, a Python-based toolbox for model predictive control. The comparison highlights a substantial reduction in computational time, with improvements ranging from two orders of magnitude in small-scale problems to a 50% decrease in larger, more complex scenarios.

A key factor in this process is the rock's permeability, which is typically estimated using the effective medium (Milton) approximation. However, this approximation relies on the assumption that inclusions are far apart, an assumption that often fails in hydrocarbon reservoirs where pockets are closely packed. To address this, we employ the Self-Consistent Field (SCF) approximation, a recently developed method that more accurately calculates the effective permeability of close-packed random suspensions. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that the SCF approximation yields significantly better estimates of effective permeability compared to both the Milton and SCF effective medium approximations when applied to suspensions with close-packed structures. Furthermore, simulations on periodic composites reveal that the SCF approximation aligns closely with exact solutions in these systems. Finally, simulations on hydrocarbon reservoirs indicate that the effective permeability calculated via the SCF approximation matches experimental data, confirming its accuracy for this specific application. These findings suggest that the SCF approximation is a robust method for estimating the effective permeability of random suspensions, even when inclusions are closely packed. This approach could prove valuable for enhancing the accuracy of hydrocarbon reservoir characterization. Additionally, the simulations presented here are suitable for implementation on a quantum computer utilizing the SCF algorithm. The source code for these simulations is available at https://github.com/AmirHosseinD/SCF-Permeability.

Although prior research has examined the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control in monolinguals and English-speaking multilinguals, almost no studies have explored these processes in Dutch-speaking multilinguals. This study investigates these processes in 12 Dutch-speaking bilinguals by comparing their reaction times and accuracy while solving arithmetic problems in both Dutch and English. The experimental design contrasted same-language trials (e.g., "2+2=4") with cross-lingual trials (e.g., "2+2=4"). Behavioral data indicated that participants were 20% more accurate on same-language trials, whereas reaction time differences were negligible. Electroencephalogram (EEG) results revealed a significant N2 component during cross-lingual trials, suggesting enhanced cognitive control, alongside a notable P3 component during same-language trials. These findings suggest that multilingualism influences cognitive control mechanisms in math-related language processing, with implications for individuals engaging in cross-lingual translation. However, EEG signal interpretation remains complex, and the limited sample size constrains the generalizability of these conclusions. Future research should expand the dataset and incorporate a monolingual control group to further elucidate these neural processes. Additionally, the current analysis focused on a specific time window; examining the full EEG data and integrating behavioral metrics would provide a more comprehensive understanding. Ultimately, these insights could inform the development of interventions to mitigate potential negative effects of multilingualism on cognitive control. Finally, a novel machine learning approach was employed to classify language based on EEG data, successfully distinguishing between Dutch and English with 70% accuracy. This method surpasses traditional behavioral measures, which showed no significant reaction time differences. These outcomes underscore the utility of EEG as a non-invasive tool for investigating multilingualism and its impact on cognitive control. Additionally, the findings support leveraging EEG data to enhance machine learning models for more accurate cross-lingual translation. Finally, the project's open-source code is accessible at https://github.com/MaxWolff/NeuralMechanismsMultilingualism.

We demonstrate that the inherent variability in human descriptions creates a misleading evaluation metric, as systems can achieve high similarity scores without accurately reflecting user needs. Furthermore, we find that descriptive features such as scene context and object attributes are underrepresented in both crowd labels and model predictions. These limitations stem from the artificial nature of current evaluation protocols, which assume that all user expectations are met simply because a description is not unanimously disliked. To address this, we propose a new evaluation framework grounded in descriptive psychology, which posits that successful description generation is context-dependent and determined by an individual's mental model of the target audience. Under this approach, the quality of a description is assessed based on the similarity of mental models between the user and the system. We validate this method through two experiments: the first involves a controlled study where participants rate descriptions of their own photographs, and the second utilizes available datasets on visual description tasks. Results indicate that this psychology-based evaluation method yields more meaningful insights into user experience and reveals distinct disparities in performance across different user groups. This evidence suggests that systems achieving top rankings in conventional evaluations may not necessarily deliver the most satisfactory descriptions in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, this work offers a more realistic evaluation strategy for image description systems and a deeper understanding of descriptive image quality. The proposed methodology is applicable to any visual description task, including photo captions, alt text, and summarization.

In many AI applications, models are trained and tested exclusively on data from a single domain, a practice that often leads to a severe drop in performance when the training and test domains do not align. For instance, image captioning models trained and evaluated on the MS COCO dataset frequently fail to generate accurate descriptions for images from the Places dataset. Such discrepancies between training and testing environments are common in real-world applications, yet they remain underexplored in existing image captioning literature. This paper examines the factors contributing to these performance gaps, with a specific focus on object attributes. We analyze images from both datasets to identify the descriptive features that cause these discrepancies, revealing that certain attributes are underrepresented in both crowd-sourced labels and model predictions. Additionally, we explore various evaluation metrics and their sensitivities to different types of descriptive features. Our analysis suggests that standard evaluation metrics are insufficient for fully understanding user experience regarding descriptive features, and that a comprehensive evaluation framework must incorporate an understanding of these attributes.

This research introduces a comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates user behavior with diffusion processes to examine how content gains visibility. The model accurately reproduces the empirical findings of citation distributions, specifically the cubic growth of concurrent citations and the long-tail distribution of total citations. By analyzing the model's diffusion and visibility metrics, we identify distinct parameter regimes that govern the growth of these distributions. Furthermore, we define an information threshold that determines whether online content gains visibility or remains obscure, and we demonstrate how varying parameters shifts this threshold. The presented models and techniques can be extended to address other phenomena related to information dissemination in complex networks.

Complex systems are frequently characterized by a few dominant components that exert disproportionate influence on collective behavior. This study investigates whether a similar principle applies to the spread of fake news, focusing on the impact of highly shared posts. We achieve this by manipulating the visibility of these top posts and observing the resulting changes in user sharing behavior. Our results indicate that top posts attract a significantly larger volume of traffic compared to others, which drives a substantial increase in overall fake news visibility. Additionally, we find that the disproportionate traffic volume is the primary factor behind the excessive sharing of these posts, rather than unique content characteristics or the presence of sensational elements. This traffic-driven effect is evidenced by the fact that even when the most visible posts are artificially replaced with random ones, users continue to share them at high rates. These findings suggest that the exceptional performance of top posts is partly due to a network effect that amplifies their reach, a conclusion that holds practical significance for platforms aiming to reduce misinformation.

In the limit where $N$ approaches infinity, we prove that the evolution of the system's one-particle distribution is governed by a specific kinetic equation. Furthermore, we explore the connection between this distribution and the Wigner limit of the quantum dynamics.

Although large-scale language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in few-shot learning, they often fail to accurately represent the specific rules they acquire from training data. We propose that a fundamental cause of this lack of interpretability lies in the complexity of the functions these models implicitly learn. To address this, we introduce a method for training state-of-the-art language models that learn simple, rule-based functions. Our approach employs a novel form of overparametrized ReLU networks trained with the Pathwise Gradient Method (PGM). PGM simultaneously optimizes both the predictive accuracy and the simplicity of the Taylor coefficients. This strategy yields models that achieve state-of-the-art performance across various natural language understanding benchmarks while capturing complete rule sets from few training examples. Although the technique is applicable to any feedforward neural network, it is especially beneficial for interpretable machine learning. To validate this, we present evidence that our method enables state-of-the-art language models to learn and display a comprehensive understanding of simple grammatical rules from as few as ten sentences. While entanglement entropy is a well-established metric for ground states of local Hamiltonians in condensed matter systems, extending it to quantum field theory (QFT) is complicated by its divergence proportional to powers or logs of the cutoff. Furthermore, entanglement entropy fails to distinguish between quantum phases. To address these limitations, Swingle and others proposed entanglement $k$-entropy as an alternative measure for local quantum many-body systems. This study investigates the behavior of entanglement $k$-entropy across two distinct phases of the double-slit experiment's quantum eraser QFT. Our findings indicate that, similar to entanglement entropy, the von Neumann entropy ($k=0$) exhibits logarithmic divergences tied to the field theory's dimensionality. Additionally, non-zero $k$-entropies ($k \neq 0$) successfully differentiate between the coherent and mixed states phases. These results demonstrate that entanglement $k$-entropy effectively characterizes quantum phases in local QFTs, complementing the insights gained from entanglement entropy.

Introduction: Quantifying the complexity of quantum field theory states is crucial for advancing our fundamental understanding of high-energy physics and developing novel quantum technologies. Entanglement entropy serves as a valuable tool for distinguishing phases in local quantum many-body systems and has been linked to black hole thermodynamics and holography. However, its direct application to quantum field theory (QFT) is hindered by its divergence, which scales with powers or logs of the cutoff. To overcome this, Swingle and colleagues introduced entanglement $k$-entropy, a quantity that not only captures complexity in many-body systems but also finite-sized black holes. Defined as a generalization of entanglement entropy, $k$-entropy retains sensitivity to quantum phases while avoiding divergences. This work examines the feasibility of using $k$-entropy to differentiate the coherent from the mixed states phase in the quantum eraser—a fundamental demonstration of the quantum erasure of interference. We find that, like entanglement entropy, the entanglement von Neumann entropy ($k=0$) scales with the dimensionality of the local quantum field theory. Crucially, non-zero $k$-entropies ($k \neq 0$) effectively distinguish the coherent states phase from the mixed states phase in the quantum eraser, confirming that $k$-entropy is a viable indicator of quantum phases in local QFTs.

We examine three distinct scenarios: (i) combining data from multiple detectors of varying individual masses, (ii) constructing a single detector from several segments, each with different masses, and (iii) constructing a single detector using segments of identical mass. Our analysis indicates that, for both scenarios (i) and (ii), the total Fisher information equals the sum of the contributions from each individual component. Conversely, in scenario (iii), the total Fisher information is approximately $\sqrt{N}$ times smaller than if the mass were distributed as in scenarios (i) and (ii), where $N$ represents the number of equal-mass segments. This reduction in information translates to an increase in the minimum detectable mass by a factor of $N^{1/4}$. These findings are general and apply to any detection method relying on gravitational wave measurements, provided that individual segments are sufficiently massive to support coherent quantum states of the test masses and are large enough to be treated as point masses. Furthermore, we observe that the total Fisher information for equal-mass segments is roughly $N$ times greater when the segments' masses are uncorrelated. Finally, we note that our conclusions regarding equal-mass segments remain valid even if a small fraction of the total mass is distributed continuously. These results assist in evaluating the optimal design parameters for future gravitational wave detectors. Scenarios involving detectors composed of equal-mass segments may become relevant if such a configuration yields a net reduction in cost or construction time. Additionally, we emphasize that our analysis relies on the assumption of a linear relationship between the detector's response and the source's mass distribution. Scenarios (i) and (ii) could arise, for instance, in a project aiming to build a 10,000-tonne detector by integrating four 2,500-tonne segments.

Machine translation (MT) enables multilingual communication, a capability that is increasingly vital in an era of global connectivity. While numerous open-source tools offer multilingual support, many fail to deliver optimal performance for specific language pairs. Although customizing MT systems can yield superior results, it demands significant time and resources, which are often scarce for low-resource languages. This paper presents a method to rapidly generate high-quality, customized MT systems for such languages by leveraging parallel text. We provide instructions for creating a system that can translate new sentence pairs with high accuracy, requiring only minutes to hours rather than days or weeks. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to produce systems with high F-score performance, even when the provided parallel text is limited.

This study presents a method for enhancing the English machine translation of Arabic text written in the Maghrebi dialects of Algeria, specifically the Tlemcen variety. The proposed approach involves creating a pseudo-parallel corpus through back-translation and combining it with an existing parallel dataset. Additionally, we introduce a technique to dynamically adjust the weight of this pseudo-parallel data during the training of a Statistical Machine Translation system. Experimental results indicate that this method significantly improves translation quality, as measured by BLEU scores, compared to systems trained solely on the original parallel corpus.

This work evaluates the performance of various machine translation systems on a newly created Basque machine translation benchmark. Basque, a language with a distinct genetic origin, is classified as severely low-resource due to the limited availability of annotated data. We compare different statistical and neural approaches, including models trained on both low-resource and richer resource settings. Additionally, we test the potential of improving these systems through parallel memory and back-translation techniques. The findings reveal that neural models outperform statistical ones, and that augmentation strategies are highly effective when substantial amounts of parallel data are available. However, when parallel data is scarce, these augmentation methods can be detrimental. Finally, we offer recommendations for future research directions regarding Basque machine translation.

While recent advancements have significantly improved performance, most approaches rely on Euclidean distance for metric learning, a choice that lacks theoretical grounding. This paper re-examines metric choice by applying information theory, demonstrating that learning in Euclidean space results in high entropy and thus poor class separation. In contrast, adopting the Minkowski distance of order 2.5 yields low-entropy outcomes with superior separation capabilities. We validate this theoretical framework with both numerical and large-scale experiments. Numerical tests compare the classification performance of various few-shot methods under different metric spaces, with results showing that the 2.5 order Minkowski distance consistently outperforms Euclidean metrics. Furthermore, experiments on the miniImageNet and fewShotOffice datasets confirm that state-of-the-art methods achieve higher accuracy when utilizing the 2.5 order Minkowski distance. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the underlying assumptions and limitations of our approach. In summary, this study offers a principled justification for preferring the 2.5 order Minkowski distance over Euclidean distance for few-shot metric learning.

# Cross-Domain Recommendation, Item-Based CF, Implicit Factor

In recent years, researchers have developed various cross-domain recommendation (CDR) systems to enable users to explore new domains by transferring preferences from others. Although many effective methods have been proposed, they often rely on transfer learning techniques that can be inefficient and prone to overfitting. To mitigate these issues, this study adopts an item-based collaborative filtering (ItemCF) approach. Specifically, the paper transfers implicit factor-based co-occurrence information from source to target domains and combines it with direct co-occurrence data. This combination occurs at two levels: first, within each domain, and second, across domains. The resulting system outperforms current state-of-the-art CDR techniques. Additionally, the implementation and evaluation can be found at https://github.com/AmirHosseinGh/ItemCF-CDR.

# 1. Introduction

MRI quality control is critical for ensuring diagnostic accuracy and maximizing clinical utility. While manual QC is time-intensive and relies on human expertise, it is often skipped in large-scale studies and research involving millions of scans. Although prior research has developed automatic QC solutions, these methods are difficult to scale effectively. This paper presents the first pipeline designed for efficient and accurate QC of massive MRI datasets.

# 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Existing Solutions and Their Limitations

Current automatic QC approaches typically depend on feature engineering and machine learning models. For instance, one method [1] uses image statistics to identify missing slices, while another [2] analyzes header data to flag orientation errors. Despite their success on smaller datasets, these techniques are inflexible and require significant domain knowledge to create and maintain.

## 2.2. Deep Learning-Based Methods

Recent efforts have explored deep learning for QC. One approach [3] trained a model to detect coil failures, and another [4] identified missing anatomy, both achieving strong results on limited data. However, these methods were developed in isolation and lack a unified framework. Their reliance on specialized, non-transferable image encoders prevents efficient processing of huge datasets.

# 3. Proposed Pipeline

We designed a three-stage pipeline to ensure both high accuracy and scalability.

## 3.1. Stage 1: Initial Filter

This stage removes scans with obvious issues, such as header data indicating missing slices, incorrect orientations, or non-human subjects. By discarding these cases early, we reduce the volume of data entering subsequent stages.

This study evaluates the DIMM's performance and scalability across various memory configurations using the Linux kernel, which streamlines deployment and facilitates large-scale testing. Our findings reveal that the DIMM achieves near-DRAM performance for sequential reads and writes, with random read latency reaching DRAM levels at higher bandwidths. Furthermore, the research offers the first open-source implementation of Near-DIMM and Beyond-DIMM architectures, allowing developers to easily utilize and assess these emerging memory solutions. When compared to traditional storage, Beyond-DIMM delivers up to 100x faster latency and 10x greater bandwidth. The results demonstrate that Beyond-DIMM can effectively replace disk storage in common workloads, delivering significant performance gains for database operations and compression-based workloads. Additionally, we present an optimized Beyond-DIMM configuration that sustains near-DRAM latency up to 100% memory utilization. Finally, the study introduces Persistent Memory Aware Scheduling (PMAS), a novel kernel scheduler designed for Beyond-DIMM environments, which delivers up to 2.5x improved latency performance over Linux out-of-the-box settings. The open-source implementation of these Beyond-DIMM architectures and the PMAS kernel scheduler are available at https://github.com/monishs/monishs-beyond-dimm.

This paper introduces a closed-loop control scheme for a class of underactuated marine vehicles featuring null damping in non-damped dynamics, specifically targeting heading angle regulation. Building upon recent findings regarding the zero-damping Euler-Lagrange system, we demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the natural dynamics of the vehicle correspond to the pendulum equation. By applying feedback linearization to decouple the fully-actuated dynamics and appropriately assigning boundary layers, we achieve asymptotic stability for the overall system. Subsequently, we employ a cascited control strategy to estimate and regulate the bounding functions, ensuring stability via a $\mathcal{L}_2$-gain condition. These findings expand the scope of marine vehicles suitable for such control techniques and offer insights into achieving bounded rendezvous times. Future work will focus on explicitly tuning these parameters to meet specific rendezvous time specifications.

We examine various microcavity configurations and identify an open cavity system as the optimal design, characterized by a moderate atom-cavity coupling of $g/2\pi = 10$ MHz and a high photon decay rate of $\kappa/2\pi = 100$ MHz. This specific system exhibits robust robustness, successfully entangling an atomic qubit with a photon and enabling reliable participation of the microcavity as a quantum memory node in a global network. Additionally, we explore extending this open cavity setup to multi-photon interactions. Finally, we assess the practical implementation of this system using InGaAsP quantum wells embedded in an air-oxide microcavity. This research offers critical design insights for microcavity-based microresonators, which are essential for microchip-integrated global quantum networks.

By utilizing these properties, we develop a fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) scheme based on algebraic geometry, which supports arbitrary nested polynomial computations involving addition, subtraction, and multiplication. ### Introduction

Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), a concept first proposed by Cryptographer Rafail Ostrovsky in 2009, enables secure cloud computing by allowing the processing of encrypted data without the need to decrypt it prematurely. This technology is particularly vital for emerging fields such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Big Data.

The primary objective of this work is to explore the potential of applying algebraic geometry to the construction of FHE schemes. We introduce an algebraic-geometry-based FHE scheme and prove its feasibility through two core properties: geometric correctness and geometric rotational inhomomorphism. The construction of this scheme is grounded in polynomial rings over finite fields.

The term "geometric" was coined in a related previous study. In this paper, we demonstrate that geometric correctness functions as the core mechanism for performing computations within the constructed FHE scheme.

To date, most FHE schemes have been developed using cryptographic methods rooted in number theory and algebraic number theory. However, the shift from integer-based to polynomial-based FHE schemes represents a significant advancement, offering superior efficiency in computation and space complexity.

While the impact of activity on radial velocity (RV) measurements is well understood, its effect on direct imaging—relying on angular resolution and contrast—is still a subject of debate. While active regions like spots and plages are known to cause RV noise, they minimally affect the integrated spectral energy distribution (SED) due to their small fractional area. In direct imaging, however, the flux from a planet is derived by subtracting the fully resolved, modeled flux of the host star from the total system flux. If active regions alter the host star's SED, they can introduce significant biases in the inferred planetary signal. We investigated how these active regions affect direct imaging by comparing a quiet Sun model to an active Sun model using a Fourier power spectrum analysis. Our results indicate that while a quiet Sun model produces noise floor-like artifacts in the planet's spectrum, an active Sun model generates complex, time-variable noise. This noise is difficult to mitigate through standard model improvements or principal component analysis and can result in false positive detections or biased mass estimates. To address this, we recommend incorporating active region proxies, such as X-ray or UV luminosity, into direct imaging analyses. This approach allows for better characterization of activity-induced noise, improving both the identification of true positives and the accuracy of planetary mass measurements. Finally, we suggest that future telescopes capable of directly imaging the Sun, such as the proposed Solar Exoplanet Transit Telescope, could provide precise data on the active Sun's SED to further refine these findings.

In recent years, there has been substantial interest in integrating Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) into wireless sensor networks (WSNs) to enhance energy efficiency. However, implementing a global, network-wide TDMA schedule is challenging due to the dynamic nature of node activity and the difficulty of maintaining an accurate, up-to-date network map. To address this, we propose a hierarchical, localized TDMA scheduling protocol that operates without requiring a global network map. This protocol is designed for WSNs where nodes are organized into clusters, each with a central aggregator. It effectively supports both periodic and aperiodic data transmissions. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our protocol surpasses existing MAC protocols, including traditional CSMA/CA, IEEE 802.15.4, and various TDMA-based schemes. Additionally, the protocol is highly adaptable to various network topologies and node mobility patterns.

This paper presents an energy-efficient, collision-free Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA) protocol for Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) that functions effectively in both ad-hoc and structured networks, handling both periodic and aperiodic traffic. The protocol operates in two modes: a standard mode for predictable, periodic data, and an extension mode for unpredictable, aperiodic data. It was tested across diverse network scenarios, including random and grid topologies with varying traffic patterns. Simulations revealed that the protocol significantly improves energy efficiency and data delivery rates compared to current MAC protocols like IEEE 802.15.4 and ALOHA, as well as other existing TDMA protocols.

Using the common marmoset monkey model, we compared the transplanted kidneys of animals that developed angiogenesis with those of control subjects that did not. Our findings indicate that the capacity for endogenous angiogenesis was directly linked to the level of injury sustained by the pre-transplant dialyzed kidneys. In marmosets exhibiting this phenomenon, there was a marked elevation in endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) within both the renal graft and the native kidneys, alongside a notable increase in vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) expression specifically within the transplanted organ. Conversely, in control-transplanted kidneys, VEGF expression remained localized to the distal tubules. These results suggest that elevated VEGF expression in the injured, transplanted kidney recruits EPCs, thereby promoting endogenous angiogenesis. This process may help explain the preservation of renal graft function and delay the onset of post-transplant diabetic nephropathy in common marmosets with endogenous angiogenesis. The mechanisms driving this angiogenesis remain unclear, but the involvement of VEGF and EPCs offers a potential therapeutic target for preventing post-transplant diabetic nephropathy. Additionally, the common marmoset model of kidney transplantation combined with pre-transplant dialysis serves as a valuable platform for investigating the etiology of post-transplant diabetic nephropathy and for testing potential therapeutic strategies. We examine the skip-gram variant, exploring how it captures a term's meaning based on its word order and proximity within a text. The goal of the analysis is to demonstrate that the resulting vector representations are robust enough to allow machine learning algorithms to derive useful knowledge. Specifically, vectors from Google News's Google News Embeddings (GNE) exhibit geometric structures that encode valuable machine-readable knowledge about American geography and politics. By interpreting GNE as a geometric graph where nodes are vector representations and edges denote relationships, we identify cycles of varying lengths that reflect patterns in how words co-occur at different distances. Our findings reveal that GNE encodes explicit knowledge, such as the sequence of U.S. presidents, as well as implicit knowledge, including the fact that Washington and Jefferson were contemporaries. These insights are derived from analyzing cycle lengths that correspond to the cyclic ordering of political figures. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these cycles enable the expression of both explicit and implicit knowledge, offering a clear interpretation of the vector space's structure. The proposed graph-based analysis framework is general and can be applied to other vector spaces to express similar types of knowledge. Finally, we provide guidance on selecting vector spaces best suited for encoding specific domains of human knowledge. The cycle analysis in this study builds upon an earlier method introduced by the authors for interpreting Google's Term Frequency/Inverse Document Frequency (TFIDF) index.

While useful for natural language computation, this approach relies on discrete representations that are incompatible with truly compositional semantics. In contrast, formal semantics for natural language typically employs a function-based model where semantic types form an ordered hierarchy; under this framework, the lexicon consists of higher-order functions that map argument types to complete interpretations. This paper demonstrates that the extended Lambek Calculus can be subsumed by a compositional semantics model featuring an ordered semantic hierarchy. Within this proposed model, the extended calculus functions as a first-order approximation, with its second-order lambda-lifting providing a mechanism for discrete lexical entry. Furthermore, this compositional semantic hierarchy offers a principled method for organizing word vectors, thereby creating a bridge between formal semantics and distributional semantics. The 2022 extension of the Hypothesis of Distributional Semantic Primacy validates this connection empirically. Finally, the model presented here aligns with the Model of Lexical Conceptual Structure, which integrates distributional and formal semantics to support computational language understanding.

-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is the ability to adapt to novel, non-stationary environments. However, most current adaptation techniques rely on the assumption that all agents will update simultaneously. This paper challenges that assumption, recognizing it as unrealistic for many real-world applications and particularly problematic for autonomous vehicles, where communication failures and varying processing speeds are common. We introduce Adaptive Multi-Agent MARL (AMA-MARL), a framework designed to enable learning and adaptation in heterogeneous, non-stationary settings. Specifically, we present Heterogeneous Opponent Modeling (HOM), which utilizes a replay buffer to capture the variability of opposing traffic. Our results indicate that combining AMA-MARL with HOM yields significant performance improvements in both short-term and long-term adaptation scenarios. While recent research has developed strategies for multi-agent systems to adapt to new, shifting joint policies, these methods typically assume that all agents update their behaviors synchronously. This assumption is often invalid in real-world scenarios, especially within autonomous vehicle (AV) contexts where communication gaps and differing processing speeds are frequent. To address this, we propose a solution where agents predict the behavior of others using a transformer-based policy network. This approach allows the system to adapt to any joint policy distribution, even when other agents do not change. Experimental results show that our method outperforms both state-of-the-art simultaneous adaptation techniques and standard reinforcement learning algorithms in both short-term and long-term adaptation tasks. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/AmirhosseinSeifizadeh/AV-Transform.

In multi-agent systems, the assumption that all participants are rational and act optimally is frequently unmet, as many agents operate with limited capabilities. To address this, we present a system that learns to adapt to the behavior of other agents. Unlike existing approaches, our method does not require all agents to update their behaviors at the same time. We demonstrate that our system achieves superior performance in both short-term and long-term adaptation compared to both simultaneous adaptation and standard reinforcement learning techniques. The CT18 collaboration aims to determine Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) and their associated uncertainties by fitting parton data to a vast collection of experimental results. These datasets span a wide range of kinematic variables, requiring the evaluation of PDFs at unmeasured points. A primary objective of this work is to develop a robust algorithm for handling uncertainties linked to parameters that are not directly constrained by the fit. This algorithm successfully produces fits with approximately a 10% improvement in uncertainty, resulting in a final product with roughly 7% smaller uncertainties than those of the most recent CT14 and MMHT PDFs. The proposed method effectively incorporates uncertainties from various sources, including experimental errors, correlations between data points, uncertainties in PDF parameters, uncertainties in cross-section calculations, uncertainties arising from uncalculated higher-order terms, and uncertainties related to unmeasured kinematic variables. The approach utilizes a sophisticated strategy to integrate over these uncertainties via Monte Carlo integration. In systems with multiple dynamic components, such as biological processes, machine performance, or economic models, identifying which factors most influence an outcome is crucial. This paper presents a method to enhance the sample efficiency of model-free reinforcement learning. By applying a multi-arm bandit algorithm to select the computational model yielding the highest rewards, the proposed approach accelerates the convergence of a model-free estimator for a previously unknown transition kernel. To address the challenge of non-i.i.d. data, a Kernelized Gradient Confidence algorithm is implemented to estimate the kernel via integral equations. As a result, the method produces more accurate estimators with fewer data points, enabling faster insights into dynamic systems. The approach is tested on two case studies: a toy simulation and a real-world analysis of computational systems using data from the 1000 Genomes Project. The results demonstrate up to a 10x decrease in computational cost relative to conventional model-free reinforcement learning techniques. Source code can be found at https://github.com/aharison/MarkovMultiArms.

For the past two decades, researchers have sought to endow machines with human-like common sense reasoning capabilities. While numerous methods have been proposed to model common sense, their application in real-world systems remains limited. We present a framework that utilizes the ATOMIC common sense reasoning database to automatically evaluate the factual accuracy of text summaries. This system achieves an accuracy of 0.60 in predicting the five most probable atomic facts for any given sentence within a paragraph, and a system-level accuracy of 0.70 in determining whether a cluster of atomic facts is supported by a specific sentence. These findings suggest a pathway for incorporating common sense reasoning into automated text evaluation and highlight a pathway for developing more robust, factually accurate text summarization techniques.

In many real-world settings, the number of training samples available for model development is limited. To address this, we propose a data augmentation strategy that leverages a large corpus of unlabeled data. Our method employs a pre-trained language model to align a small dataset with an extensive unlabeled corpus, followed by the application of contrastive learning to refine the model's representations. We validate our approach across three natural language understanding (NLU) tasks: intent classification, slot filling, and text classification. Results indicate that our technique effectively improves performance on all three tasks. Additionally, the system demonstrates strong performance in ranking sentences by similarity to a query, achieving a mean reciprocal rank (MRR) of 0.841 on the HotpotQA dataset.

We propose a generalization of the well-known "hard covering" technique to accommodate these specific limitations and utilize it to derive an achievable inner bound for the capacity. By applying specific modifications and assuming high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, we determine the precise asymptotic ergodic capacity under both Rayleigh and Rician fading environments. Furthermore, the general approach yields a method for designing $\mathsf{MIMO}$ downlink codes. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed codes achieve a non-trivial asymptotic ergodic capacity even at low SNR values when the number of transmit antennas exceeds the number of receivers. Additional numerical results explore the asymptotic ergodic capacity within an interference channel context. The study also includes extensions to scenarios involving mixed power constraints and point-to-multipoint $\mathsf{MIMO}$ channels. Finally, we present an overview of how this technique applies to maximizing capacity in $\mathsf{MIMO}$ broadcast channels within both single-cell and multi-cell settings under these constraints. Although numerous computational methods have been developed to analyze Hi-C data, selecting the most appropriate tool for specific datasets or biological questions remains challenging. This work presents a new software solution to address these challenges.

The simulated flow encompasses the complete evolution of the jet, from ignition through the potential core, outer recirculation zone, and mixing layer, down to the sub-grid scales. To validate the simulations, several diagnostic metrics are employed to assess flow development and structure, including mean and turbulent quantities, turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) budgets, turbulence intensity, Froude numbers, and the turbulent Prandtl number. Additionally, the simulation data is compared against experimental results.

This database serves as a benchmark for validating subgrid-scale models in Large Eddy Simulations (LES) and for investigating the fundamental physics of jet flames.

We demonstrate that varying the strength of randomness induces a transition from a phaseseparated state to phase mixing. This process is governed by the interplay between the interaction strength within homogeneous phases and the surface tension between different regions. In the XXZ spin model, this transition shifts from first order to second order as the system dimension increases. We also examine how this transition unfolds in the Hubbard model across the first few dimensions. Furthermore, we explore the influence of finite linear system size and surface effects on these dimensional transitions. The analysis relies on a combination of the effective medium approximation and a systematic expansion in powers of surface area. In higher dimensions, the model exhibits a transition from phase separation to phase mixing, which can be first or second order depending on the specific model and dimensionality. As dimensionality rises, the nature of this transition shifts from first to second order. In lower dimensions, the boundary between separating and mixing phases is determined by surface tension, whereas in higher dimensions, it results from an interplay between the internal interaction strength of the phases and the surface tension. We analyze the potential of direct detection experiments to identify UHE cosmic ray-induced long-lived massive particles. We examine two scenarios: (i) dark matter production through multi-nucleon dissociation and (ii) pair production as a final-state radiation effect. Our results show that for a universal nucleon-dark matter coupling, dark matter masses above roughly 100 GeV are constrained by the non-detection of flux depletion in UHE cosmic rays. Conversely, if high-energy cosmic ray nucleons have a non-universal coupling to dark matter, limits from direct detection experiments become stronger. In this case, dark matter masses greater than approximately 10 GeV are ruled out by the flux depletion criterion, and the resulting mass limits align closely with those from direct detection experiments. We compare our limits on UHE cosmic ray nucleon-induced massive particle production with existing constraints from other production mechanisms, including neutrino telescopes, air shower arrays, and gravitational wave observations. Our study demonstrates that the non-observation of flux depletion is a powerful tool for investigating new physics in the multi-TeV energy regime.

Recent observations of gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers have spurred interest in using neutron star properties to test gravitational theories. We demonstrate that nonlocal modifications to the Einstein-Hilbert action, characterized by two unknown parameters, are constrained by the recently measured properties of the most massive neutron star, PSR J0740+6620. These properties place a lower bound on the total mass in a binary merger, which, when combined with gravitational wave data, restricts the parameter space of nonlocal gravity. We find that the growth of cosmic structures in this framework is slower than in Einstein gravity, implying a universe without dark matter or dark energy. This model also fails to account for superclusters and massive black holes. However, recent findings on the abundance of low-mass galaxies at high redshifts suggest that these structures can exist under certain conditions within nonlocal gravity. These results indicate that binary neutron star observations are crucial for validating or refining constraints on the theory, particularly when combined with other high-redshift data such as gravitational wave signals. Furthermore, we note that recent claims regarding constraints from GW170817 and NICER data may have overlooked the available parameter space.

Replication is a fundamental technique in large-scale distributed systems, and determining where to store these replicas is both a critical and intricate problem. This paper introduces a novel approach to this challenge, focusing on systems with multi-domain architectures where replication goals and constraints vary across different domains. This approach employs a graph-based placement strategy, termed Rhea, which operates through two distinct mechanisms: intra-domain and inter-domain placement. Rhea was developed to support Facebook's data storage infrastructure, known as Ceph. Rhea has been implemented and successfully deployed to replicate up to 10 copies of objects across up to 10 different data centers. Evaluation results show that Rhea achieves performance comparable to hand-tuned placement strategies while being 100 times less computationally expensive.

In distributed systems, deciding where to store replicated data is a crucial challenge. This report examines the replication decisions made by Google's Filestore service. We explore the trade-offs involved in balancing performance, fault tolerance, and operational simplicity. Furthermore, we outline the design decisions made at Facebook regarding data replication and compare them with Google's strategies.

This paper explores the complexities of data placement in distributed systems, a decision that significantly impacts both system performance and energy efficiency. Subsequently, we present an extensive collection of real-world systems that utilize various placement policies, a resource that is often lacking in existing literature. We identified extreme coldspot sequences associated with transcription factor binding and nuclease cleavage, as well as extreme hotspot sequences linked to transcription factor binding, nucleosome positioning, and DNA shape. Furthermore, extreme hotspots were found to be enriched in non-coding regions of the human genome. The derived local mutation tolerance scores are accessible at http://localmutationtolerance.cbcb.umd.edu/.

Genomic variants can influence human health through multiple mechanisms, and their effects are often difficult to predict. Integrating data from random mutation assays with local mutation tolerance scores enables a more comprehensive prediction of variant impact. We identified variants with extreme tolerance scores within the ExAC database and observed that extreme coldspot variants are significantly overrepresented in loss-of-function categories, whereas extreme hotspot variants are overrepresented in benign categories. Extreme tolerance scores were also found to be enriched in variants associated with specific human diseases. Consequently, incorporating mutation tolerance scores can help refine the interpretation of genomic variants.

However, this hypothesis faces significant challenges, primarily the absence of observed or inferred optical counterparts. In this study, we apply the 2MASS Point Source Catalogue v.2 to identify all sources within 1 parsec of the Galactic Centre towards 2.2 $\mu$m that exhibit variability consistent with the X-ray sources in question. Our analysis reveals that the variable sources are almost entirely composed of the brightest and most massive main-sequence stars in the Galactic Centre, characterized by effective temperatures exceeding 15,000 K and masses greater than 6 M$_{\odot}$. Consequently, these objects are unlikely to host an intermediate-mass black hole primary or to be magnetars. Instead, the variability observed in these sources is almost certainly attributed to accretion from evolved stellar wind companions. This finding implies that the X-ray sources identified by G2GC and previously identified in the Galactic Centre are predominantly evolved binary systems. These systems could potentially be identified as the magnetically powered X-ray transients proposed in recent works, and their discovery would offer a pathway to constrain the existence of accreting magnetars. Furthermore, these variable sources may constitute a previously unrecognized class of X-ray transients, which could significantly impact current models of Galactic Centre X-ray emission. Our results confirm the previously observed Gaussian distribution and extend the upper limit of dark matter in the Galactic halo to 2.5%. Furthermore, we constrain the maximum density of dark matter clumps that could interact with WB stars to 0.01 M$_\odot$. These findings significantly tighten the bounds on dark matter interactions with WB stars, reinforcing the conclusion that the Milky Way's stellar halo is unlikely to contain any substantial amount of dark matter. Additionally, we note that the characteristic velocity dispersion of the solar neighborhood is consistent with a distribution of relative velocities for WB stars with intermediate separations. Finally, we observe that the velocity distributions of systems with both small and large separations are inconsistent with the King potential, which is commonly employed to model Galactic halo dark matter. This inconsistency is attributed to Galactic tides and the finite size of the WB star sample. We also place constraints on the density of dark matter clumps interacting with WB stars with very large separations, which are comparable to the limits derived from their velocity distributions. Ultimately, we determine that the velocity distribution of WB stars with intermediate separations is consistent with a Gaussian distribution, which is only possible in an empty universe. In summary, our study provides robust constraints on the density and total mass of dark matter clumps interacting with WB stars possessing intermediate semi-major axes.
