Multivariate point processes are widely used to represent systems where occurrences at one location or time influence future events, offering applications in telecommunications, seismology, ecology, and finance. However, scaling these models to extensive datasets with rich, high-frequency information can be challenging. While thinning methods exist, they may lead to inaccurate inferences in certain scenarios. This research examines an alternative: process regression. We evaluate the circular autoregressive process of order $p$ ($CARP$), a model designed to capture univariate peak-and-surge dynamics in isolated time series, as a component of a thinned, observed, multivariate point process. Although process regression is a recognized technique for reducing the intensity of such processes, it can suffer from inference bias when applied to scaled processes with peaks. By comparing traditional thinning against process regression, we determine that process regression yields more accurate inferences for the total number of events and the peak-to-surge ratio in certain cases. Although process regression is not universally superior, it provides a valuable option for researchers working with scaled point processes where precise inference is critical.

is a widely used Lagrangian method for simulating fluid flows involving free surfaces, yet it faces challenges in accurately resolving flows near solid boundaries due to incomplete kernel support near the surface. This study presents a novel approach to resolve such flows by treating the solid boundary as a no-slip wall and employing ghost particles to model the fluid on the solid side. These ghost particles are initialized at the same positions as wall particles and are assigned velocities matching the wall particles. To ensure accurate pressure calculations and force transmission, the pressure and force exerted by wall particles on nearby fluid particles are computed using the formula $F_{ij} = -\nabla_i W(|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j|, h) \cdot P_j S_j A_j$, where $P_j$ and $A_j$ denote the pressure and area of particle $j$, and $S_j$ is a shape factor. Crucially, the force from a wall particle on a fluid particle is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the force from the fluid particle on the wall particle, satisfying Newton's third law. This technique was implemented in a two-dimensional SPH code to validate its accuracy. The results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively resolves two-dimensional fluid flows near solid boundaries using SPH. Furthermore, the flow characteristics of a two-dimensional circular cylinder at a Reynolds number of 200 were examined. By adjusting the number of ghost particles, the study successfully reproduced the von Kármán vortex street, with the shedding frequency aligning closely with Strouhal's law. Finally, the computational efficiency of this method was compared against existing approaches for two-dimensional fluid flows near solid boundaries. This research was conducted during the author's tenure as a JSPS Postdoctoral Fellow for Early-Stage Researchers. The code is available at https://github.com/hiroyuki-ko/SPH.

To create robust models capable of withstanding attacks, it is essential to understand how feature extractors process visual data. This paper introduces a novel, generalizable method for reverse-engineering feature extractors, which has been applied to analyze ResNets, VGG, and Inception networks. Our approach begins by placing a random classifier at the end of the extractor and iteratively optimizing an input image to match the labels of specific target objects. The resulting images, or ghost images, allow us to reconstruct the entire mapping of the extractor. These maps were evaluated using two distinct metrics. Experimental results indicate that the visualization maps of VGG and ResNet(50) contain more semantic information than those of Inception(v3), and that deeper extractors generally capture richer semantic content. # Reverse-Engineering Feature Extractors and Visualizations

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have significantly advanced computer vision, yet their feature representations remain difficult to interpret, hindering efforts to build robust systems. This work presents a new approach to evaluate the semantic richness of CNN features. We develop a reverse-engineering method to reconstruct the mapping of a feature extractor, which in turn enables the creation of visualization maps rich in semantic content. Our methodology was tested across various classifiers and extractors. Our findings demonstrate that deeper CNNs capture more semantic information in their higher layers, and that VGG and ResNet extractors are superior to Inception in this regard. Additionally, we introduced a new image optimization method to generate visualization maps. These maps were scored using two distinct evaluation metrics. The scores indicate that visualization maps from deeper layers contain more semantic information, and our method outperforms existing techniques. We also conducted a user study to assess the perceptual meaningfulness of the maps. The results confirm that our generated maps are indeed perceptually meaningful to humans.

We also investigate the potential of these high-charge-per-pulse beams for diverse fields, including medical therapy, free-electron lasers, laser-plasma accelerators, and astrophysics.

Neutrinos are among the most abundant massive particles in the universe, influencing cosmic evolution through their free-streaming nature and impact on structure formation. While current neutrino mass limits from particle physics and direct detection are in the sub-eV range, cosmological constraints are already tighter, currently restricting the sum of neutrino masses to $\sum m_\nu < 0.12$ eV at 95% confidence. Upcoming experiments aim to probe masses as low as 0.02 eV, yet foreground contamination remains a critical challenge for such precision. This paper explores how foregrounds affect CMB parameter estimation, with a specific focus on neutrino mass constraints. We conducted simulations using realistic foreground maps with diverse scanning strategies and advanced foreground removal algorithms. Our analysis reveals that these current methods produce scale-dependent biases in the small-scale CMB temperature power spectrum, resulting in significant neutrino mass biases of $\Delta(\sum m_\nu) \sim 0.015$ eV at small scales and $\Delta(\sum m_\nu) \sim 0.005$ eV at large scales. These effects are most pronounced at high frequencies and large Galactic latitudes, representing a critical consideration for future experiments designed to place stringent constraints on neutrino mass.

This work extends the results from [10] by utilizing a coordinate system with reduced regularity, which is compatible with null-C^3 normal coordinates. Ultimately, this coordinate system enables the extension of rectangular domain findings to a semi-circular domain, although it does so within a space of lower regularity. We introduce a method to assess the bias of language models by analyzing their textual outputs. The proposed test suite, which offers a broad array of bias challenges, is constructed using contrastive data from human annotators. Moreover, we find that fine-tuning for specific tasks can inadvertently increase a model's bias, a phenomenon that can be partially mitigated through the use of unbiased training data. We provide a website for exploring these findings at https://bias-testers.github.io/.

Most current research concentrates on the global path planning phase, overlooking the potential for multiple seemingly optimal paths to encounter obstacles during local execution. While magneto-optical trapping allows for the laser cooling of atoms to low temperatures and microglass field strengths, its sensitivity is ultimately constrained by the trapping potential's depth. This study introduces a novel technique capable of measuring magnetic fields as low as 100 picotesla, surpassing the sensitivity limits of magneto-optical trapping. The proposed method utilizes a pulsed optical lattice to temporarily enhance the sensitivity of a magneto-optical trap, enabling Ramsey spectroscopy on otherwise unreachable hyperfine states. This approach was demonstrated with Rubidium-87, and a theoretical framework is presented for applying the technique to other alkali atoms. Furthermore, the research explores how optical feedback can increase optical lattice pulse energy, thereby further improving detection sensitivity. Beyond its immediate significance for precision measurement and manipulation of trapped atoms, this method offers a versatile tool for exploring other microscopic interactions. Additionally, the strategy of combining Ramsey spectroscopy with magneto-optical trapping could facilitate the detection of DC magnetic fields within the 100 picotesla to 100 microtesla range using ultracold atoms possessing accessible low-field sensitivity. Finally, the paper examines the potential of optical feedback to elevate the overall trapping potential, potentially by an order of magnitude, which could be crucial for implementing the mentioned Ramsey technique. The work concludes by considering the combination of optical feedback, optical molasses, and magneto-optical trapping to create an optical dipole trap, potentially enabling the study of two-component Bose-Einstein condensates.

In recent years, spin squeezing has garnered substantial interest for its potential to surpass the standard quantum limit in atomic measurements. This letter demonstrates that, specifically for ultracold Rubidium-87 atoms, spin squeezing can be generated via parametric spin interactions induced by a Raman transition between two hyperfine states coupled to a single off-resonant laser mode. This technique offers a straightforward pathway to achieve spin squeezing with minimal experimental complexity. We present a model that calculates the necessary parameters to produce measurable spin squeezing, and we propose an experimental implementation that requires only minor adjustments to existing optical molasses setups.

We demonstrate that the standard two-photon Ramsey method can be significantly improved for detecting weak magnetic fields by employing a superposition of two harmonic oscillator states. This combination allows for sub-microtesla sensitivity across a broad frequency range (from 10 Hz to 100 kHz), thereby overcoming the limitations inherent in traditional trapped-ion and atomic trap-based sensors.

Heterostructures exhibiting this intrinsic MCE could also serve as sensitive thermometers for detecting minute temperature gradients. This work underscores the significance of the intrinsic MCE in such systems for next-generation magnetoelectronics and spintronics. In contemporary dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic, the Calculus of Constructions (CC) stands as a foundational type system. Developed by Gérard Huet in 1980 and refined by Thierry Coquand in 1985, CC has driven decades of innovative work in proof assistants and safe programming. However, many existing reconstructions of CC are either outdated or lack formal verification. This work introduces `CC-Coq`, a formally verified and concise reconstruction of CC implemented in Coq. It also presents an equally formal explanation of key type-checking concepts, such as dependent types, equality, and unification. The `CC-Coq` reconstruction has been integrated into the Smallfoot type checker, a component of the larger Yoneda platform, enabling the checking of types for Agda programs.

Type unification is a critical component of most practical type systems, serving as the foundation for features like type inference and overloading. Within the simply typed lambda calculus, unification is linear and resolved in linear time. More complex systems, however, rely on higher-order unification, which is generally non-linear and undecidable. Modern type checkers therefore employ heuristics to guide unification toward sound approximations that support powerful type system capabilities. This paper formally defines higher-order unification, examines various unification strategies, and evaluates their effectiveness as approximation algorithms within a commonly used fragment of Martin-Löf Type Theory. The findings demonstrate that several decades-old unification algorithms produce sufficiently precise type approximations for these types.

Software development relies heavily on libraries and frameworks, which are so extensive that even experienced developers may lack a complete understanding of their attributes and object attributes. While many approaches exist to represent attributes and inheritance through ontologies, they typically fail to incorporate data derived from actual object attributes. To overcome this, we propose a method for constructing a software ontology that begins with a set of initial concepts and develops an ontology structure grounded in the attributes of real instances. We have implemented this approach to build a .NET ontology, validating its effectiveness. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this method can be generalized to create ontologies for any software library or framework.

**Introduction**

Instance segmentation masks provide detailed information about individual objects within point clouds, supporting various 3D vision applications. While recent implicit neural methods have shown promise in generating textured 3D textures and per-vertex attributes like color, these approaches typically struggle with creating accurate 3D instance masks. We propose an alternative method that produces sharper results by leveraging the global frequency information inherent in Fourier transforms.

**Background**

**Neural Point Cloud Representations**

Implicit neural representations utilize neural networks to map spatial coordinates to attributes, enabling the prediction of properties for arbitrary 3D points. For instance, MinkowskiEngine (Wu et al., 2019) employs hash grid representations of 3D space to process point clouds efficiently. Similarly, PointNet (Chen and Gupt, 2017) processes point clouds through point-wise fully connected layers. These techniques have been successfully extended to predict attributes such as color and orientation.

**Fourier Features**

Fourier features were originally introduced to enhance the expressiveness of neural networks for continuous input domains (Vasilevskiy et al., 2020). They have also proven effective in rendering textured images from 2D point correspondences (Barron et al., 2021).

Galactic Center exhibits characteristics of both active galactic nuclei and starburst galaxies, making it an ideal environment to investigate their combined influence on the evolution of circumnuclear gas and dust. Utilizing the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA), we conducted a comprehensive census of dust condensations within the Galactic Center's most dense molecular environment. Our analysis identified 1,100 sources with masses ranging from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{2} M_{\odot}$ and distances between 290 pc and 1 pc from the center. By employing a simple coreless model to characterize these sources, we derived their formation and evolution rates across various distances. The results indicate that both the formation and evolution rates of these sources peak at a distance of 1 pc from the center. Furthermore, the average source mass increases as the distance from the Galactic Center grows. These findings suggest that the extreme conditions in the Galactic Center, characterized by intense radiation and shocks from the starburst, drive the formation of low-mass sources at small distances, while the presence of an intermediate-scale molecular torus facilitates the accumulation of mass at larger distances. Additionally, the prevalence of these sources at all observed distances suggests they can serve as viable progenitors for planetary systems. Finally, the substantial number of these sources in the central parsec offers a potential explanation for the unexpectedly high mass of the central black hole. This study represents the most extensive investigation of star-forming sources in the Galactic Center to date. The derived source distribution and evolution rates provide valuable insights for understanding the evolution of star-forming regions in the dense molecular gas surrounding other active galactic nuclei and starburst galaxies throughout the universe. A primary reason for this reliance is the pervasive illusion of expertise displayed by AI recommendation systems; by showing users only results that align with their past behaviors and preferences, these systems create a selective reality that reinforces existing biases. This effect is especially pronounced in critical domains like healthcare, where individuals often accept recommended doctors without question, even when those recommendations are driven by narrow metrics like historical visit frequency rather than clinical excellence. To address this, we introduce the concept of search engine transparency, which involves disclosing the origins of recommended items and flagging potential biases in both the engine and the user. To demonstrate the challenges of achieving this transparency, we examine case studies from major search engines and propose practical methods for implementing it. Furthermore, we highlight that ensuring search engine transparency is inextricably linked to the need for explainable AI, offering a foundational step toward building more trustworthy algorithms. The search transparency framework presented here is designed to guide researchers, engineers, and policymakers in advancing transparent systems across various fields. Search transparency can also serve as a benchmark for evaluating future AI safety and trustworthiness initiatives, ultimately fostering a culture of explainability within the AI industry. The accompanying code repository provides a demonstration of search transparency using ElasticSearch.

Search engines are integral to modern life, yet they are frequently misused because their results are often irrelevant to users' actual needs. While many web applications leverage search functionality, they rarely offer user-friendly mechanisms to express complex information needs. Although query reformulation can enhance search outcomes, users must invest significant effort to learn how to construct effective reformulations. To mitigate this burden, automatic query reformulation systems can generate multiple iterations of queries and retrieve corresponding results, thereby improving overall relevance. However, there is a risk that these systems may inadvertently lead users down unproductive paths. To illustrate this potential issue, we analyze several query reformulation case studies and demonstrate how, even with some successful retrievals, the process of reformulation can be misleading. Consequently, we argue that search applications should incorporate visual indicators to alert users when query reformulation is being used and to contextualize its impact.

Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensors are increasingly integrated into autonomous systems, offering a cost-effective means to monitor wildlife. While recent studies have shown that deep learning models can identify and track animals in LiDAR data, they often lack robustness when processing noisy data, and existing tracking algorithms struggle with partial point clouds. The method leverages the unique characteristics of LiDAR data, combining the predictive capabilities of data-driven models with statistical techniques to ensure robustness against noise and sparsity. Our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms on public LiDAR tracking benchmarks and is computationally efficient, enabling real-time operation.

A positive definite function, $f: G \to \mathbb{C}$, on a group $G$ is one where the matrix $(f(g_i g_j^{-1}))_{i,j=1}^n$ is positive definite for all $g_1, \dots, g_n \in G$. This article investigates positive definite and complex symmetric matrices, with a specific focus on those that satisfy additional positivity conditions. We identify necessary and sufficient criteria for a block matrix to be complex symmetric and demonstrate how to construct its associated positive definite matrix. Furthermore, the block circulant matrix arising from this development is examined in detail. Its associated positive definite matrix exhibits remarkable structural properties, such as being block lower triangular with diagonal blocks that are positive definite. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between positive definite functions and Schur multipliers, investigating the closure of the range of a positive definite function under the Hadamard product. Finally, we explore the connection between positive definite functions and group representations. Specifically, any positive definite function on a finite group that has an irreducible representation can be expressed as a linear combination of the matrix coefficients of that representation. Additionally, a positive definite function on a finite group is completely determined by its values on group elements corresponding to transpositions. These transposition-based functions are both necessary and sufficient to ensure that the sum of their products with non-negative complex coefficients yields a positive definite function. These findings hold promise for theoretical advancements and practical implementations, particularly in statistics, machine learning, and signal processing. In this context, we examine microcanonical lattice gas ensembles near their first-order phase transition point by computing the tilting potential and the probability current. Our findings indicate that both the tilting potential and the probability current remain finite near the transition point, thereby validating the existence of a finite-step latent heat and a vanishing kinetic friction. Additionally, we introduce a modification to the thermodynamic identity, demonstrating its consistency with established results from statistical mechanics. These outcomes provide robust support for the completeness of the microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics framework when dealing with finite systems undergoing phase transitions. Furthermore, this study offers a rigorous foundation for formulating finite-system phase transition theory and reinforces the necessity of employing the microcanonical ensemble in such analyses. Finally, the established microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics for finite systems creates a robust platform for developing nonequilibrium critical exponents and renormalization group theories specifically tailored to such systems.

We examine the nonequilibrium phase transition of the two-dimensional Ising model under a transverse magnetic field using the microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics framework. By utilizing the tilting potential and probability current, we identify a lambda-type latent heat. Our results demonstrate that both the magnetic field strength and the tilting potential are finite at the critical point, which confirms that the latent heat exhibits a power-law behavior. Moreover, we find that the thermodynamic identity holds without modification in this scenario. These findings not only validate the applicability of the microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics framework to the two-dimensional Ising model under a transverse field but also underscore the significance of the microstate approach for constructing a comprehensive nonequilibrium thermodynamics theory for finite systems.

We further investigate the two-dimensional Ising model under a transverse magnetic field using the same microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics methodology. Our analysis reveals that both the tilting potential and probability current are finite at the critical point, indicating that the latent heat follows a power-law distribution. This result allows us to determine the critical exponent for the latent heat. We also verify that the modified thermodynamic identity is satisfied. Consequently, we conclude that the fractional part of the one-cycle loop of the probability current constitutes the latent heat in finite systems. These findings provide a solid foundation for formulating nonequilibrium critical exponents and renormalization group theories within the microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics framework.

However, recent investigations have revealed that the attention mechanism employed in the Stack attention model closely mimics an aligned source language character sequence. This model utilizes a set of translated target language characters, generated by attention over the source language, as memory to facilitate translation. Machine translation aims to convert text from one language to another. Furthermore, translational medicine was noted to be particularly vulnerable to the reproducibility crisis affecting the broader scientific community. While the term "translational medicine" is now widely recognized, it is argued that the field itself remains underdeveloped. To address this, the concept of translational medicine is defined as a combination of fundamental and clinical investigations targeting the same disease, which is presented as a "sum of parts" approach. This definition is contrasted with alternative frameworks such as "disease-oriented science" and "precision medicine." Although these approaches do not strictly require translational research, they focus on developing advanced clinical capabilities and personalized treatments, respectively. Although these methods have yielded significant successes, they have inadvertently neglected the foundational fundamental research essential for understanding complex diseases. Consequently, a framework for fundamental translational research is proposed, with an emphasis on developing research questions, hypotheses, and validation strategies that span from fundamental mechanisms to clinical applications. The discussion concludes by examining how these research paradigms influence funding priorities and the development of research infrastructure. Finally, it is reasoned that a robust translational medicine field requires a balanced integration of all three research approaches. While a unified framework for translational medicine is not presented, it is believed that a deeper understanding of the distinct roles and interconnections between these research types will facilitate the development of a robust translational medicine research enterprise. This research was supported by the National Institutes of Health.

Diseases are frequently categorized as either infectious or genetic, yet this binary classification overlooks the significant overlap where environmental factors influence disease expression in individuals with specific genetic predispositions. To address this, a framework is introduced that classifies diseases based on the level of predictability in their phenotypic outcomes. Within this model, rare diseases with highly predictable phenotypes are termed "single-cell diseases," whereas those with unpredictable outcomes are labeled "population diseases." This framework is applied to fundamental research strategies, including reverse genetics, genetic mapping, and quantitative trait locus analysis, to illustrate how different research paradigms are utilized to study both single-cell and population diseases. It is demonstrated that a strong research program often requires a translational approach, integrating research focused on both single-cell and population diseases. Additionally, the discussion highlights how research into single-cell diseases can yield fundamental insights applicable to the development of diagnostics and therapies for complex population diseases.

The primary objective of this study is to develop an explanation framework for end-to-end neural scoring models that employs a counterfactual approach to identify and highlight scoring-relevant words. By integrating this interpretability mechanism, a model of any architecture can generate explanations that are as accurate as the model itself. Unlike previous methods that rely on sparse sampling or backpropagation to surface relevant terms, the proposed framework produces thousands of counterfactual counterparts for each essay to pinpoint key words. Specifically, it identifies the shortest sequence of counterfactual edits required to transform an input essay into a counterpart with a known score. These sequences are then ranked based on the information theory importance of the words they contain. Experiments conducted on a dataset of middle-school student essays scored by an LSTM-based scoring model show that the proposed method yields more generalizable and accurate explanations than existing techniques. Additionally, human evaluations confirm that the generated explanations are both comprehensible and meaningful to end-users. Cancer detection via digital pathology is crucial for diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. Although digital pathology offers numerous advantages, its reliance on expert pathologists has led to concerns regarding inconsistent diagnosis quality. Pathology-based computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems have been widely explored to assist pathologists. However, to ensure robustness and reduce the risk of misdiagnosis, pathological CAD systems should deliver diagnosis diversity alongside accuracy. In this study, we introduce a new contrastive learning strategy to facilitate diagnosis diversity. Our framework, the multi-label diagnosis network (MLDN), employs a dual-encoder structure to extract both visual and natural language representations. A multi-label classification network then produces diverse diagnosis predictions based on these learned representations. To achieve a balance between diversity and accuracy, we utilize a large dataset of natural language reports to train a contrastive loss function. This loss is applied during inference to produce diverse predictions from a single image. Experiments conducted on the PASCAL-PRO and CAMELYON3D datasets confirm that our method successfully provides diagnosis diversity, offering more reliable and comprehensive support for cancer detection.

Reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to train an agent to maximize cumulative rewards, but the field lacks a rigorous understanding of how exogenous factors influence this process. We examine Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with exogenous state variables and rewards to identify conditions under which reliable learning remains possible. Specifically, we introduce the concept of "exact" states to define a class of MDPs with exogenous exogenous rewards where the agent can achieve an unbiased estimate of the policy's return. Our research reveals that an "exact" estimator can be derived when exogenous exogenous rewards are additive, exhibit a reward shaping effect, and are time-invariant. We also explore scenarios where exogenous exogenous rewards are non-additive or time-variant, offering insights into modifying these exogenous components to achieve an unbiased learning outcome.

We investigate Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) containing exogenous state variables and rewards to establish a framework for understanding their impact on learning. Within this framework, we define a class of MDPs with exogenous exogenous rewards where the agent can learn the policy's return without bias. We demonstrate that an "exact" estimator is achievable when exogenous exogenous rewards are additive and have a reward shaping effect, even if they are time-variant. Moreover, we show that an "exact" estimator can be learned when these exogenous exogenous rewards are non-additive or time-variant, provided the rewards can be made additive through a particular reward scaling method.

By utilizing computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems, radiologists can achieve more reliable and consistent tissue characterization. However, because biological tissues are heterogeneous, their mechanical properties vary significantly. Consequently, deep learning models trained on limited datasets struggle to generalize when encountering tissues with atypical structures or properties. To address this challenge, we propose a novel uncertainty quantification approach for deep learning-based ultrasound elastography. This method employs Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) with variational inference to identify regions of interest (ROIs) that are difficult for the model to classify. The proposed transformation method relies on four key components: first, a recursive algorithm to assign polynomial-order weights to subformulas within sequents; second, an inversion rule for sequent calculus operators that preserves these weights; third, a set of transformation rules that convert sequent calculus proofs into BiNormalForm while adhering to weight constraints; and finally, a collection of rewrite rules that normalize the resulting proofs into BiNormalForm. The application of this method has been implemented in the proof assistant Coq. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how proof complexity metrics, such as depth, can be defined based on normalized weights and employed to specify proof normalization rules. In the concluding section, the authors outline directions for future research.

### I. Introduction

Contrastive learning has recently emerged as a potent unsupervised technique, proving highly effective across various machine learning domains. By learning representations through unlabeled data, it enables models to adapt to new tasks with minimal additional samples. Despite these advantages, the complexity and computational intensity of current contrastive learning frameworks limit their practical utility. This study focuses on streamlining the application of such methods for few-shot classification.

Few-shot classification involves categorizing inputs with only a limited number of training examples. Although model performance typically degrades as the number of training samples per class decreases, recent advances have shown that pre-training on unlabeled data can significantly boost final accuracy. Building on these findings, we propose that contrastive learning offers a viable pathway to enhance few-shot classification performance.

Although contrastive learning is conceptually straightforward, existing implementations remain complex and resource-intensive. For instance, the widely adopted SimCLR [1] requires extensive data augmentation, large mini-batches, and multiple GPU clusters. Similarly, MoCo [2] depends on maintaining memory banks to generate negative samples, necessitating substantial computational resources. In this work, we demonstrate that the core principles of SimCLR can be effectively applied to few-shot classification with greater efficiency and simplicity.

The primary contributions of this paper are:
1.  A streamlined version of SimCLR tailored for few-shot classification, which eliminates the need for memory banks and data pre-processing.
2.  Empirical validation showing that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques across multiple few-shot classification benchmarks.

**Introduction**

A key challenge in multi-task reinforcement learning is the ability to generalize to new tasks that are similar to those encountered during training. While recent research has shown that agents can successfully generalize to tasks within a close neighborhood of their training distribution, they may over-generalize to tasks far outside this neighborhood when trained on a diverse set of problems. To mitigate this issue, we restrict the agent's generalization capability to a defined neighborhood by incorporating a regularization term into the multi-task objective. This term is derived from a similarity metric that estimates the proximity of a new task to the training distribution.

**Related Work**

Our research builds upon and extends the methodologies presented in *Multi-Task Actor-Critic for Reinforcement Learning* and *Generalization Bounds for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning*.

Experimental results confirm that the acceleration achieved via partial solutions performs as well as that from complete solutions and is compatible with even the slowest MRF models. Consequently, this method enables faster and more efficient real-time image restoration. In summary, the proposed acceleration technique is both general and robust.

In recent years, deep learning has enabled impressive image reconstruction from corrupted inputs, including tasks like deblurring, dealiasing, deconvolution, denoising, super-resolution, and single-image refocusing. These problems are typically ill-posed, often yielding multiple possible solutions. To address this, researchers have developed regularized optimization frameworks that impose constraints to select the most plausible solution. Despite these advancements, solving the resulting optimization problems remains computationally expensive, hindering real-time applications. This report presents a method to reduce computation time by approximately an order of magnitude. The proposed approach involves training a deep learning model to predict the optimal Lagrange multipliers for the regularization terms within the optimization formulation. By inputting a corrupted image into this network, the inference of the regularized image's optimum becomes significantly faster. This report evaluates the method on several regularized optimization models and different regularized image restoration challenges. Results confirm that the predicted optimal regularized images closely match those obtained from exact optimization, with only minor differences in regularization parameters. The reported computation time reduction exceeds an order of magnitude.

This study introduces a random access protocol utilizing slotted ALOH with fixed transmission power. The protocol's key parameters, specifically the number of retransmission slots and transmission power, are optimized based on channel conditions to maximize system throughput. To evaluate performance under varying power levels, both numerical analysis and simulations were conducted. The results indicate that fixed power transmission yields lower throughput compared to power control methods, though it remains viable for small networks. Throughput optimization is identified as highly sensitive to THz path loss, which is influenced by the operating frequency and material properties. To mitigate this, the research proposes utilizing rough surfaces to manipulate wave propagation. Finally, the proposed protocol is analyzed in the context of indoor THz communication, with a focus on optimizing user mobility and spatial density. This comprehensive examination provides essential insights for the practical deployment of future THz networks.

Terahertz (THz) communication is essential for supporting expanding connectivity needs and overcoming existing backhaul and front-haul limitations. However, uncoordinated random access in THz networks presents unique challenges due to severe free-space path loss, atmospheric absorption, and dense user distributions. To ensure reliable access, this paper proposes a coordinated random access protocol based on directional beamforming. The protocol employs a multi-tier beam training mechanism to establish synchronized communication and an adaptive beam alignment procedure to maintain synchronized links. To prevent interference during the training phase, random access slots are designed with directional THz sub-channels created by specific combinations of azimuth and elevation angles. To ensure the protocol's reliability, the authors derive an upper bound on concurrent users per sub-channel and determine optimal random access and multi-tier beam training parameters. These parameters are calculated using a multi-objective optimization framework that accounts for access probability, concurrent user limits, and throughput. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed protocol achieves high access reliability and significant throughput.

The rapid advancement of wireless communication technology has spurred extensive research into next-generation wireless systems, with Terahertz (THz) frequencies emerging as a critical enabler for ultra-high data rates and low-latency applications. Despite the potential of THz communication, random access protocols face unique hurdles, including limited spatial reuse, high path loss, and atmospheric absorption. This paper examines random access challenges within an interference-limited, multi-user, multi-hop THz ad-hoc network featuring directional antennas. It evaluates the impact of antenna beamwidth and distance on network performance and develops a Markovian model to assess spatial reuse

We identified four distinct screens, three of which were previously known, and determined that three of the four likely formed before the last glacial maximum, with at least one forming before the mid-Pleistocene transition. The fourth screen is very young, possibly having formed as recently as a few hundred years ago. We also report new estimates for the mass and other properties of these screens. Finally, we constructed a model for screen formation based on the statistical distribution of observed screen ages. This model indicates that screens form via the gravitational collapse of pre-existing density fluctuations, with the typical mass of these fluctuations increasing over time. Consequently, the majority of screens formed in the current era are too young to detect, implying that the four screens we have detected are likely not representative of the full population. This finding aligns with the observed power law distribution of scattered pulse arrival time variances. Furthermore, the inferred increase in typical mass over time suggests that the power spectrum of the primordial density field may have been scale-dependent, potentially indicating the influence of massive neutrinos. However, the constraints derived from this model are not strong enough to definitively rule out a scale-independent spectrum. Ultimately, the distribution of screen ages offers a promising avenue for future research into the early universe.

Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental to modeling physical phenomena, and recent advances in deep learning have introduced universal operators capable of solving broad classes of PDEs. This work presents a unified framework for learning and solving parabolic PDEs with respect to spatial variables, supporting problems with diverse boundary conditions, source terms, and initial conditions. By leveraging a single operator trained on partial problems, the method achieves a generalization error of $O(N^{-1.5})$ in the $L^2$ norm for test equations on a grid with $N$ points, a result supported by rigorous theoretical analysis.

We examine the application of deep operator networks (DeepONets) to a specific class of parabolic partial differential equations. Our approach involves training the network on a collection of initial conditions and source terms to predict the solution at a target time $T$. We provide convergence analysis showing that DeepONets achieve spectral accuracy for this problem class. Notably, the network exhibits high generalization accuracy across a wide range of initial and source functions, even when these differ significantly from those used during training.

This work investigates the use of deep operator networks (DeepONets) for solving a specific category of parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs). The method is trained on a set of problems defined by source terms and/or initial conditions to predict the solution at a designated time $T$. The primary contribution of this study is the theoretical analysis of the network's generalization capabilities. Analytical proofs demonstrate that the network can achieve spectral accuracy when applied to initial value problems within a designated function class, characterized by sufficiently high regularity.

However, the influence of a host star's metallicity on a planet's ability to retain an atmosphere and sustain liquid water remains unclear. This study examines the effects of both low and high metallicity on the atmospheric and climatic conditions of Earth-like planets within their habitable zones. Our findings indicate that while low metallicity results in only minor climatic changes, high metallicity significantly alters surface pressure, temperature, and the liquid water zone. Specifically, high metallicity causes the liquid water zone to shift closer to the surface and expand in width, while simultaneously increasing the likelihood of runaway greenhouse and snowball Earth scenarios. These effects are more pronounced for planets around high metallicity stars, as the enhanced irradiance from the stellar wind and charged particles drives atmospheric loss. Consequently, the suitability of high metallicity stars for hosting habitable Earth-like planets remains uncertain. These conclusions are derived from one-dimensional climate models and should be validated through future three-dimensional simulations. Additionally, the observed metallicity impacts on surface pressure and the liquid water zone may aid in refining exoplanet detection methods.

The search for habitable worlds has revealed a vast array of exoplanets, prompting the need to assess their potential for life. This assessment relies on understanding how stellar characteristics, such as activity levels and metallicity, affect planetary climates. While the activity of G-type stars can trigger extreme events like runaway greenhouses or global freezes on Earth-like planets, the consequences of orbiting stars with different metallicities remain unclear. This review examines the current understanding of how a host star's metallicity influences the surface pressure and liquid water zone of an Earth-like planet in its habitable zone. We conclude that high metallicity is likely detrimental to surface liquid water, whereas low metallicity has minimal impact. These insights are based on recent climate modeling studies, which should be corroborated by upcoming three-dimensional simulations. The results presented here may guide the selection of targets for future direct imaging missions, such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

This distinction is achieved by modifying the superconducting order parameter's symmetry in 2D systems hosting magnetic impurities through an external in-plane magnetic field. Our findings indicate that under a finite in-plane magnetic field, the MBS zero-energy peak vanishes, whereas peaks arising from Kondo effects or quasi-particle tunneling become more pronounced. Additionally, we demonstrate that MBS are fragile in the presence of disorder; even a small amount of randomness in the impurity distribution causes the MBS peak to disappear as the distance from the vortex core increases. These results provide a means to distinguish MBS signatures from other zero-energy peaks in non-slab 2D superconductors with magnetic impurities via local tunneling conductance, a configuration relevant to recent experimental observations. We further show that in the strong coupling regime, both MBS and quasi-particle tunneling peaks are suppressed by an exchange interaction between magnetic impurities and conduction electrons. Finally, we note that in the weak coupling regime, MBS are more robust against the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction than quasi-particle tunneling peaks. These conclusions regarding MBS robustness hold for both 2D systems with isolated magnetic impurities and those with domains of aligned spins. The disappearance of the MBS peak due to exchange interaction or disorder is more gradual than that caused by the exchange interaction alone. This study offers a roadmap for both theoretical investigations and experimental efforts to confirm the existence of MBS in non-slab 2D superconductors with magnetic impurities, such as Fe/InAs quantum corrals.

While many studies have focused on developing detection models to identify various flaw types, there remains a scarcity of research on creating an optimized detection system. We observe that achieving this requires not only identifying the source's position but also verifying the presence of emitting cues, such as visible vocal cords or mouth movements. To address the scarcity of annotated data, we introduce a new dataset featuring over 10,000 images with tight bounding boxes for both the sound sources and their cues, which will support future end-to-end training. For the immediate goal of validating spatiotemporal validation, we propose a simple yet effective method that integrates temporal validation signals into our existing single-image estimator. However, most existing GCN approaches are constrained to homogeneous graphs, where all nodes and edges share the same weight type, thereby limiting their versatility. In contrast, real-world data often forms heterogeneous graphs with complex structures, rendering current methods inadequate for accurately modeling these intricate relationships. This paper introduces a novel range-based heterogeneous graph convolutional network (RHCN) designed to efficiently process and classify heterogeneous graphs. The RHCN achieves this by aggregating features from connected nodes within a local neighborhood, utilizing a mechanism that differentiates edge types through a type-specific weight type. Furthermore, it employs a convolution operation tailored to these heterogeneous types to integrate neighbor information effectively. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that RHCN is equivalent to a multi-linear operation, which can be efficiently executed using matrix operations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets confirm that RHCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both feature learning and node classification tasks. The RHCN framework is implemented in PyTorch and is accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuan1995/RHCN.

Starting with a Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) in a magnetic field within a $\left|F=1, m_{F}=-1\right\rangle$ state in a linear trap, we implement a Raman cooling cycle using a Raman laser to maintain a BEB in a dark state, $\left|F=1, m_{F}=-2\right\rangle$. By modulating the aspect ratio of the linear trap, we shift one end of the BEB into a parabolic trap, where a second Raman photon elevates the atoms to the $\left|F=1, m_{F}=-1\right\rangle$ state. Through careful tuning of Raman cooling and trapping parameters, we successfully loaded a parabolic trap with approximately $1.5 \times 10^{8}$ BEB atoms at a rate of $2.5 \times 10^{6}$ atoms per microsecond. This high-rate, high-number, and high-fidelity loading of a parabolic trap paves the way for precision measurements, such as electric dipole moment searches, that demand extreme spatial separation between atomic samples and magnetic field gradients. This represents the first demonstration of transferring a BEB to a parabolic trap via a two-state Raman cooling cycle. The reported loading rate, to our knowledge, exceeds all previous single-species, BEB-to-parabolic-trap transfer rates by an order of magnitude. Additionally, the final BEB number and trap depth achieved in our hybrid trap configuration surpass the capabilities of standard magneto-optical and parabolic-magneto-optical traps, respectively.

While computational methods have been developed to support pathologists, few solutions effectively account for heterogeneous tissue samples containing mixed benign and malignant regions. We contend that models trained on such diverse samples suffer from performance degradation due to class imbalance, and that simply increasing training data from these mixtures exacerbates the problem by amplifying imbalance. To investigate this, we conducted extensive experiments across multiple datasets, varying both the quantity and proportion of normal versus cancerous tissues. Our results confirm that data imbalance is the primary cause of performance issues, particularly when models are trained on samples with low cancer content. Finally, we examined the impact of inconsistent histological staining, showing that although state-of-the-art models are generally robust to such variations, performance becomes unreliable without sufficient data from various staining conditions. These findings offer critical insights for designing and executing histopathological studies involving tissue microarrays.

To address the high expense and time constraints of expert annotation, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has emerged as a promising solution. UDA enables models trained on labeled source domains to generalize to unlabeled target domains. However, most existing approaches rely on heuristic assumptions about domain correspondence, which can lead to significant performance drops when these assumptions are incorrect. To overcome this, we introduce a novel uncertainty-guided domain adaptation framework that automatically identifies and leverages uncertain predictions during testing to locate target domain data with high source domain similarity. This allows the model to focus on adapting to specific areas of uncertainty rather than relying on potentially flawed assumptions regarding domain similarity. Extensive experiments on three histopathology datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, even in scenarios with large domain shifts. Source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyux/UNCERTAINTY-GUIDED-DOMAIN-ADAPTATION-FOR-HISTOPATHOLOGY.

We conducted a comprehensive study on the electronic and magnetic properties of monolayer $\text{MnTeSe}$ using first-principles calculations. By varying the Se/Te ratio, we identified a critical point where the system transitions from an antiferromagnetic to a ferromagnetic state. This transition is driven by a shift in the majority-spin $d$-band filling, which is controlled by the Se/Te composition. Conventional machine translation methods treat each sentence in isolation, which hinders performance on complex structures and restricts the system's ability to learn and correct errors during translation. Conversely, end-to-end (EE) methods, which have recently emerged, allow for simultaneous text correction across multiple levels, including ST. Despite their superior accuracy, EE systems currently lack the capacity to handle domain-specific vocabulary, a critical requirement for many practical applications. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a post-processing framework that maps EE system output to domain-specific terminology. This mapping is achieved through a combination of edit distance and character-level translation. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields a significant reduction in Untranslated Word (UW) errors and a substantial improvement in overall BLEU scores. Furthermore, the framework effectively manages out-of-vocabulary words, a common challenge in EE systems. We have deployed this solution in a live production environment for news translation. Evaluation metrics confirm that our system outperforms the previously used conventional machine translation system. Additionally, the paper discusses various design considerations and lessons learned from implementing this solution in production.

**Category:** Machine Translation

**Introduction**

This section outlines the problem definition, presents a high-level overview of the speech translation system, and details the proposed enhancements.

**Problem Definition**

Speech Translation (ST) is the process of converting spoken audio from a source language into written text in a target language. In recent years, End-to-End (EE) models have been developed for ST, offering the distinct advantage of performing target text correction simultaneously with translation. These EE models enable the correction of issues such as untranslated words, mistranslated terms, punctuation, and capitalization errors. However, a key limitation of current EE models is their inability to map to domain-specific vocabulary, a constraint shared by most existing ST systems. To address this, we have designed a post-processing framework that translates EE system output to domain-specific terminology.

**High-Level Overview of Speech Translation System**

A standard ST pipeline typically consists of three main stages: Acoustic Modeling, Language Modeling, and Decoding. Acoustic Modeling involves training an acoustic model on audio and text data to map source language audio to target language text. Language Modeling trains a model on monolingual target language data to refine the translation probabilities. Finally, Decoding combines the acoustic and language models to generate the final translation.

) for image super-resolution (SR) has become a standard approach, leveraging large, high-quality, low-resolution (LR) images to produce sharp SR outputs. However, such datasets are often heterogeneous, resulting in inconsistent SR quality across different regions. This inconsistency poses significant challenges for downstream applications, such as super-resolution in medical imaging. To address this, we introduce a joint adversarial and adaptive weighting (JAAD) framework designed to enhance the homogeneity of LR-to-SR mappings within heterogeneous image collections. The proposed method comprises two primary stages: (1) an unsupervised clustering phase that categorizes LR images into distinct groups based on their potential semantic content, and (2) an SR network training phase that employs an adaptive weighting strategy to enforce consistent LR-to-SR mappings across these diverse image spaces. The effectiveness of our approach is validated on two heterogeneous image databases, the Bridge and the Multi, demonstrating superior LR-to-SR mapping homogeneity compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, the consistency of the resulting SR images is confirmed through evaluation in downstream tasks, including tissue classification and cell segmentation. The JAAD framework is versatile and can be integrated with various single-image SR architectures to achieve homogeneous LR-to-SR mappings in diverse image collections. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedshafey/JAAD.

While Particle Mesh (PM) gravity offers a computationally attractive framework for calculating gravitational potentials, it fails to account self-acceleration induced by the cosmological constant. Although Jaffe's modified PM method resolves this issue for isolated particle collections, it introduces inaccuracies when multiple clusters are present due to non-vanishing contributions from distant particles. This study introduces a straightforward approach to incorporate the effects of an expanding universe into the PM method for collective self-gravity assessments. The proposed technique determines the expansion-related contribution to the Newtonian potential using only a few terms of the Green's function series, thereby ensuring high accuracy even when particle distributions overlap. Validation through numerical experiments demonstrates that the new method achieves an error margin of less than 0.1% with approximately 10^9 particles across four distinct distribution scenarios. Furthermore, the method requires minimal additional computational resources compared to the standard PM approach, making it particularly advantageous for simulations involving multiple overlapping clusters, such as those modeling cosmic web structures or the entire universe. Consequently, this work provides a precise and efficient solution for investigating the effects of self-accelleration in cosmological simulations. Consequently, this approach enables more accurate computation of physical quantities derived from the gravitational potential, including the non-linear growth of large-scale structures and the evolution of dark matter halos within an expanding universe.
